name: Tor Browser fingerprint-resistance model (aka Tor Browser Bundle; the 'one fingerprint for all' / uniformity model; ancestor of Firefox privacy.resistFingerprinting)
kind: Browser feature set plus a written design document (The Design and Implementation of the Tor Browser), shipped as a Firefox ESR fork. Not a content extractor.
maturity: Production, continuously maintained since 2008. The design document's Cross-Origin Fingerprinting Unlinkability requirement is the stable normative core; individual defenses (letterboxing 2019, RFPTargets-era granularity) churn per ESR cycle.
license: MPL 2.0 for the Firefox-derived code, BSD 3-clause for tor itself, with bundled fonts under their own free licenses. Permits use in this project without restriction; the practical bar is operational, not legal.
keeps_and_discards: Not an extraction approach: it keeps the entire DOM and discards nothing from the document. What it discards is environment entropy on the way IN. Canvas readback is blocked or returns a placeholder unless the user grants per-site permission, font enumeration is restricted to a bundled set, screen/window dimensions are quantised, timezone is forced to UTC, locale to en-US, media devices and WebRTC are suppressed, and performance timers are coarsened (~100ms). At the Safer/Safest security levels NoScript disables WASM/JIT and then JavaScript entirely for HTTP(S), at which point a JS-built page yields only its server-sent markup. That last mode is the only one that changes what content survives, and it changes it catastrophically for SPA content.
structure_preserved: Full DOM nesting, ordering and tabular relations are untouched at Standard security level; Tor Browser does not rewrite the document. Shadow boundaries behave exactly as in upstream Firefox: open roots are traversable, closed roots are not, and Tor adds no mechanism for reaching them. At Safest level, structure that only exists because scripts built it is absent from the tree entirely, so the observed structure is the server-sent structure, not the composed one. Letterboxing does not alter the DOM; it alters the visual viewport, which changes computed layout and therefore anything downstream that reads geometry.
interactive_elements: No special handling. Controls are ordinary DOM nodes and are preserved verbatim. At Safer/Safest, controls whose behaviour is script-attached are still present as markup but inert, which produces a silent divergence between 'element looks interactive' and 'element does anything'.
interactive_state_fidelity: Fully preserved at Standard level because nothing is removed: disabled, checked, selected, aria-expanded, aria-checked and the rest of the ARIA state surface are exactly whatever the page set, and both the DOM and the accessibility tree reflect them. The token cost is not Tor's to pay; it is paid by whatever serialiser reads the tree. The real fidelity hazard is the security slider: at Safest, script-driven state (aria-expanded flipped by a click handler, checked set programmatically) never occurs, so the captured state is the initial-parse state and is silently wrong rather than absent. [uncertain] No published measurement of ARIA-state divergence across Tor security levels exists.
layout_awareness: Deliberately layout-perturbing rather than layout-reading. Letterboxing rounds the content window to a multiple of roughly 200x100 CSS px and adds visual margins, so innerWidth/innerHeight, media queries, and every geometry read (getBoundingClientRect, IntersectionObserver, scroll extents) are quantised. It reads no page geometry itself; it constrains the geometry the page can observe.
javascript_required: No, and it is the one option here that can be run with JavaScript wholly off. At Standard level scripts run normally and page telemetry fires as usual. At Safest level scripts do not run at all, so no telemetry fires from the page — but neither does any client-rendered content exist. There is no middle setting that runs layout without running analytics; the granularity is per-security-level, not per-script.
evaluation_method: Requirement-driven rather than benchmark-driven. The design document states adversary model and requirements (Cross-Origin Identifier Unlinkability, Cross-Origin Fingerprinting Unlinkability, State Separation, Long-Term Unlinkability) and each defense is argued against them. Empirical evaluation happens outside the project: EFF Cover Your Tracks, AmIUnique/Panopticlick-lineage entropy studies, and academic fingerprinting surveys. There is no fidelity or extraction benchmark because extraction is not the goal.
corpus_size_and_origins: No fixed corpus. Web-compatibility regressions are tracked by bug report and by the Tor Project's own site-breakage issue queue, not by a frozen page set. Third-party entropy measurements that Tor's uniformity claim leans on (Panopticlight/AmIUnique lineage, ~hundreds of thousands to low millions of self-selected volunteer submissions) are self-selected, privacy-interested populations and therefore not representative of the general web population. Any 'Tor users are indistinguishable' figure inherits that sampling bias.
reported_precision_recall: Not applicable in extraction terms. The relevant published figure is anonymity-set size / fingerprint uniqueness, and Tor's design claims approximate uniformity within a security level and platform bucket rather than a numeric rate. [uncertain] No current peer-reviewed measurement of the residual within-Tor-Browser fingerprint entropy at a stated ESR version was located.
independent_oracle: Partially. EFF Cover Your Tracks and AmIUnique are operated independently of the Tor Project and do not share its implementation assumptions, which makes them a genuine external check on uniqueness. They are, however, self-selected-population instruments and they measure the attributes they chose to measure, so they cannot certify absence of a novel vector. Network-layer identification (exit-node IP lists) is an oracle Tor cannot defeat and that no fingerprint test reports.
evidence_independence: Mixed. Design rationale is first-party (Tor Project). Uniqueness measurements are third-party academic or EFF. Breakage evidence is user-reported and therefore neither first-party nor systematic.
page_archetype_coverage: Uneven and asymmetric to the usual extraction split. Static article and documentation pages survive every security level. Product, listing and collection pages that depend on client-side rendering degrade at Safer and vanish at Safest. Service pages (login, checkout, anything CAPTCHA-gated) fail before content is reached, because Tor exit IPs draw the heaviest challenge rates on the web. Forum pages sit in between. There is no published per-archetype figure; this is a structural prediction from the mechanism, not a measurement. [uncertain]
script_and_locale_behaviour: Actively locale-hostile by design: locale is forced to en-US and timezone to UTC regardless of the user's real settings, and the bundled font set is chosen for uniformity rather than script coverage. CJK, Indic and RTL pages therefore render with fallback fonts and can produce different line-breaking and different shaping than a native browser, which perturbs any geometry-derived signal. Text content itself is unaffected — the DOM strings are the DOM strings — so a text-only fold is script-invariant here while a geometry-reading one is not.
leaks_outward: Minimal to the page and heavily minimised to third parties: state is partitioned by first-party domain, third-party cookies are blocked, referrers are trimmed, and all traffic exits via the Tor network so the origin server sees an exit-node address rather than the operator's. What it does leak is the fact of being Tor Browser, which is a strong and deliberate signal. Note this is exactly inverted from the local measurement context: reading the saved corpus makes roughly 3,082 external requests per run to 92+ distinct hosts, and Tor would route every one of those through the network rather than eliminate them.
mechanism_detectability: High and actively exploited in production, but at a different layer than the ones this project worries about. Tor Browser announces itself three ways that anti-bot vendors demonstrably act on today: (1) exit-node IP membership, which is a published list that Cloudflare, Akamai, DataDome and PerimeterX all consume and which reliably triggers interstitial challenges or outright 403s; (2) the RFP artifact set — quantised window dimensions that are exact multiples of the letterbox step, UTC timezone with en-US locale on every profile, a bundled font list, coarsened performance.now() resolution — each of which is a positive tell rather than an absence; (3) canvas-permission-prompt behaviour, where a blocked or placeholder canvas readback is itself distinguishable from a real one. The important consequence for the stated tension: Tor's own defenses do not hide automation, and running the sensor behind Tor would make the session MORE conspicuous, not less. Compare this with Marionette/geckodriver, whose principal tell is navigator.webdriver === true — a single boolean that is checked ubiquitously but is a far narrower signal than exit-IP membership.
countermeasures: The security slider (Standard / Safer / Safest) is the only user-facing dial, and it trades content fidelity for script surface monotonically. Bridges and pluggable transports address network-layer blocking of Tor itself but do nothing about exit-IP reputation on the destination side. There is no supported way to keep Tor's fingerprint uniformity while shedding the Tor-ness signal; the two are the same mechanism.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not measured by the project and not measured publicly in extraction terms. The only relevant local anchor is the hardening-arm result already held: a null control gives a 0.07% fold-drift floor, and block_trackers costs 10.49% on live sites against 0.16% on saved pages. Tor at Standard level would be expected to sit closer to the tracker-blocking end on live sites because third-party blocking and state partitioning both suppress network-dependent content; Safest would be a different order of magnitude entirely because client-rendered content disappears. Neither has been measured here. [uncertain]
gate_state_at_capture: Worst-in-class and directly relevant. Tor exit IPs draw disproportionate CAPTCHA and consent-interface rates, so a Tor-routed corpus systematically over-samples the gated state. With roughly 67% of top sites showing a consent interface even from a clean residential path, a Tor-routed capture pipeline that does not record gate state will silently produce a corpus dominated by challenge pages and consent walls rather than content. Tor Browser records nothing about gate state itself; that would have to be instrumented by the caller.
determinism: High within a version and security level, and higher than upstream Firefox by construction — that is the point of uniformity. Quantised dimensions, fixed timezone and locale, and a fixed font set remove most sources of run-to-run variation in anything geometry- or environment-dependent. Content determinism is unchanged from upstream: a page that renders differently per request still does.
determinism_across_versions: Poor across ESR boundaries. The letterbox step, the bundled font list, the set of RFP-covered targets and the coarsening granularity have all changed across releases, and each change moves every geometry-derived and environment-derived value at once. Anything keyed on window dimensions or font metrics should be treated as version-scoped, not stable.
reproducibility: A capture is reproducible only if the exact Tor Browser build, security level, and the page's own stability are all pinned. Exit-node rotation means the origin sees a different client address each circuit, so geo-varied content and rate-limit state are not reproducible at all. There is no frozen corpus.
failure_modes: Origin-side blocking of exit IPs (403, endless challenge); CAPTCHA walls that consume the capture; script-dependent content missing at Safer/Safest; font-fallback-driven layout divergence on non-Latin scripts; per-site canvas permission prompts stalling automation; and consent interfaces appearing more often than baseline. Circuit-level latency also inflates any timing-sensitive readiness heuristic.
failure_visibility: Mixed, and the dangerous half is silent. Network blocks and CAPTCHAs are loud (non-200 or an obviously wrong document). Content missing because JavaScript did not run at Safest is silent — the fold returns a well-formed, plausible, and wrong tree. Letterboxing-driven geometry shifts are also silent. This is precisely the silent-degradation pattern the project refuses, and it argues against running captures at any level above Standard.
scale_limits: Throughput is the binding constraint: Tor circuit bandwidth and latency put a hard ceiling well below direct fetching, and aggressive parallelism is both slow and reputationally self-defeating (more exit-IP flags). Cost stops being linear in the number of concurrent captures long before it does in page size.
delta_cost_model: None. Tor Browser has no incremental-update notion; it is a browser, and every capture is a full page load. It neither helps nor hinders an O(delta) design directly, except that circuit latency makes re-fetching (the fallback when a delta cannot be computed) markedly more expensive, which raises the value of a working delta path.
reanchoring_stability: Neutral — node identity is whatever the DOM gives, and Tor changes nothing about it. One second-order effect: exit-node rotation can land a re-capture on a different geo-variant or A/B arm of the same URL, which presents to a re-anchoring layer as a large spurious content change with no corresponding mutation. That would inflate a measured re-anchor rate for reasons that have nothing to do with the anchoring scheme.
adversarial_exposure: Does not help. Tor preserves invisible-to-human content exactly as the page authored it: zero-width and tag characters, off-screen and display:none nodes, HTML comments and JSON-LD all survive untouched. It has no notion of concealment. The one indirect effect is negative for this project: letterboxing quantises the viewport, which shifts which nodes are 'outside the visible area' — and viewport-based hiding accounts for 1,802 of the concealed injections catalogued in the 2026 in-the-wild study, so a letterboxed viewport changes the ground truth of that category rather than filtering it.
provenance_carrying: None at the representation level. Tor provides no per-token origin, no capture-time stamp, no shadow-depth marker. It does supply one provenance fact the caller could record: the security level and browser build in force at capture, which determines whether script-built content could have existed at all. That belongs in a capture-envelope field, not in the fold.
roundtrip_safety: Not applicable — there is no serialisation step to round-trip. Tor neither escapes nor normalises document text.
token_budget_and_ordering: No influence. Tor imposes no truncation, no ordering, and no context policy. The only second-order effect is at Safest level, where the absent script-built content changes what there is to budget for.
representation_cost: No change to tokens per page at Standard level; the document is the document. At Safest the token count drops sharply on client-rendered pages, and every token saved is a token of real content, which is the wrong trade.
what_could_be_adopted: Three transferable ideas, none of them the browser itself. First, the uniformity-over-randomisation argument: if this project ever normalises the capture environment, it should pick one fixed profile shared by all runs rather than per-run jitter, because jitter is itself a fingerprint and it destroys determinism. Second, the security-slider discipline: an explicit, recorded, discrete hardening level attached to every capture, so a corpus can never silently mix hardening states — this maps directly onto the existing hardening-arm measurements. Third, letterboxing as a warning rather than a feature: it demonstrates that quantising the viewport changes which content counts as visible, which is exactly the coupling the no_layout_in_the_fold constraint is trying to avoid, and it validates keeping geometry in the peripheral.

constraint_violation_ledger.verdict: Negative oracle only, with one adoptable-in-the-actuator-layer element (the recorded discrete hardening level).
constraint_violation_ledger.structure_agnosticism: No conflict. Tor applies no structural heuristic and names no region. Neutral.
constraint_violation_ledger.no_layout_in_the_fold: Conflict, indirect. Letterboxing perturbs the geometry peripheral and shifts viewport-visibility ground truth. It does not put layout in the fold, but it makes the peripheral version-dependent and quantised. Actuator-layer concern.
constraint_violation_ledger.o_delta: No support and mild antagonism. No incremental model at all, and circuit latency raises the cost of the full-refetch fallback.
constraint_violation_ledger.no_mocks: Fully compatible and in fact exemplary — it is a real browser end to end. The Safest security level is the exception: disabling JavaScript makes the captured page a different artifact from the real one, which is a stub by another name and should be treated as violating the spirit of no_mocks in any measured path.
constraint_violation_ledger.closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: Fully consistent. Tor offers no attachShadow patching and no privileged shadow access; closed roots remain closed. It is the strongest confirmation available that the project's refusal is the mainstream posture.

governance_signal_handling: None. Tor Browser sends no bot-identifying signal, does not read robots.txt, has no AIPREF or Content Signals awareness, cannot participate in Web Bot Auth (it has no signing identity and the whole point is to have no stable identity), and would receive an HTTP 402 as an opaque error. Routing through Tor is in direct tension with the emerging authenticated-agent regime: Web Bot Auth rewards a stable, attested identity, and Tor is engineered to destroy exactly that.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Tor changes the operator's exposure, not the lawfulness of the act. Under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 the regulated act is collecting and persistently storing personal data from public sources, and that is unchanged by the transport. Anonymised transport arguably worsens the legitimate-interest balancing rather than improving it, because it removes the controller's ability to be identified and contacted, which the Guidelines treat as part of transparency. Tor retains no PII of its own and adds none to the artifact.
